extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, juries, and litigating counsel in patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials covering inequitable conduct (duty of candor, materiality, intent), damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty), date damages begin, and the factors for calculating damages (Panduit factors and reasonable-royalty/hypothetical negotiation factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory jury use and verdict form structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Court may try equitable issues with an advisory jury; if using an advisory jury, decide whether to charge the jury on the entire issue or only materiality and/or intent to deceive issues. Verdict form should have separate questions on each issue charged (materiality, intent, and/or balancing equities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inequitable conduct is alleged based on failure to disclose to PTO, courts should carefully consider using an advisory jury because of complexity: inequitable conduct defense is under clear-and-convincing/elevated standard while the 'but for' PTO issuance issue is under preponderance (Therasense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and definition of inequitable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants have a duty to prosecute patent applications before the PTO with candor, good faith, and honesty. This duty extends to all named inventors, patent attorneys/agents involved, and any other individual substantially involved in prosecution. Intentional failure to meet this duty is 'inequitable conduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequitable conduct arises from intentional failure to meet duty of candor (withholding/misrepresentation/submission of false info).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct – elements and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish inequitable conduct the defendant must prove by the highly probable standard (clear-and-convincing level) that (1) an individual with duty of candor withheld or misrepresented information, or submitted false information material to examination, and (2) that individual acted with specific intent to deceive or mislead the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Therasense and related Federal Circuit precedent; both materiality and specific intent must be proven by the elevated standard; identify each asserted basis for defense in instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality — 'but for' standard for non-disclosure cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is material if 'but for' the failure to disclose or misrepresentation, the PTO would not have allowed one or more claims — i.e., more likely than not the PTO would have refused one or more claims had it been aware of the withheld/true information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To decide, use the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim(s) under consideration and apply the more-likely-than-not standard as the PTO would. If this standard shows PTO would not have allowed claims, the withholding/misrepresentation is material even if the claims might still be invalid in the lawsuit; defendant still bears overall burden to prove inequitable conduct by the highly probable standard. (Therasense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality — affirmative egregious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant alleges affirmative egregious misconduct (e.g., perjury, filing an unmistakably false affidavit, fabricating evidence, deliberate schemes to defraud PTO) and you find by highly probable standard that such conduct occurred and rises to egregiousness, then the misconduct is material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of egregious misconduct: perjury, fabricated evidence, deliberate schemes. Examples of non-egregious acts: mere nondisclosure of prior art or failure to mention prior art in an affidavit. (Therasense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to deceive — specific intent standard and inference rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If material information was withheld/misrepresented or affirmative egregious misconduct occurred, determine whether it was done with specific intent to deceive or mislead the PTO. Intent may be shown by direct evidence or inferred from facts/circumstances, but only if the single most reasonable inference from the evidence is that the individual acted with intent to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot infer intent solely from materiality (even high materiality), from lack of a good-faith explanation, from gross negligence, or negligence. Must determine the individual knew of the information, knew it was material, and made a deliberate, conscious decision to withhold or misrepresent it. Consider totality of circumstances and whether conduct occurred in good faith. (Cites Therasense and multiple Fed. Cir. cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general standard and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If accused device/method infringes any valid asserted claims, determine damages to compensate the plaintiff. Plaintiff must prove each element of damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Damages must compensate plaintiff to put it in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement; damages may not be punitive or include interest as an extra addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A damage award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. Instructions about damages do not indicate which party should win; they are guidance if jury finds for plaintiff. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 284 and Federal Circuit precedent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin — Alternate A (stipulated notice date)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the parties stipulate the date that plaintiff first notified defendant of infringement, that stipulated notice date is the start date for damages calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may agree on 'infringement notice date' and use it as damages start date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin — Alternate B (disputed notice date, product claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the date of notice is disputed, plaintiff must prove by preponderance that defendant was actually notified on the date alleged. Notice can be given either by (1) public marking (marking substantially all products with 'patent'/'pat' and patent number or internet marking), which starts damages when marking began, or (2) specific notice to defendant about alleged infringement, which starts damages when defendant received that notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff and licensees did not properly mark substantially all products and did not notify defendant specifically before suit, plaintiff can only recover damages after filing date. Internet marking is acceptable if labeling links to a posting connecting product to patent number. If adequacy of marking is at issue, additional instructions required. (Cites 35 U.S.C. § 287 and case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin — Alternate C (lawsuit filing date)
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicable, damages begin on the date this lawsuit was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use filing date when marking/notice methods did not timely give notice to defendant. (Cites statutory and case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary damage types — lost profits and reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent damages fall into two categories: lost profits (the additional profits plaintiff would have made 'but for' the infringement) and reasonable royalty (the reasonable payment for use of the invention). Reasonable royalty is the minimum recoverable amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If lost profits not proven (or only proven for a portion), jury must consider reasonable royalty for remaining infringing sales. Brief definitions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — 'but-for' test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost profits, plaintiff must show by a preponderance that, but for defendant's infringement, plaintiff would have made additional profits from sales (in whole or part) of the accused products; jury must determine what customers would have done absent the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits at issue are plaintiff's lost profits, not defendant's profits on infringing sales. (Cites relevant Federal Circuit precedent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factors — framework for proving lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff proves lost profits by establishing each of the four Panduit factors by more-likely-than-not: (1) demand for the patented product; (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; (3) plaintiff's manufacturing and marketing capacity to make the lost sales; and (4) amount of profit plaintiff would have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court explains each factor in subsequent instructions and provides case citations (Panduit and Federal Circuit cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor — demand for the patented product
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand shown by significant sales of plaintiff's patented product or significant sales of defendant's accused product (if sufficiently similar and competing in same market). Do not consider sales driven mainly by advertising/marketing or unpatented features as evidence of demand for the patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales of defendant's products may be used only if products are sufficiently similar to compete; include supporting case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor — absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether non-infringing substitutes existed that were acceptable to actual buyers; if competitors could have captured sales with substitutes, plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must offer one or more advantages important to actual buyers, not infringe the patent, and have been available during the damages period (competitor must have had equipment, materials, know-how). If some customers would likely have purchased substitutes, plaintiff has not shown entitlement to those sales. Even if only plaintiff and defendant had the advantageous features, plaintiff still must prove it would have made defendant's sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor — market share allocation when substitutes exist
rubrics_metrics.description: If acceptable non-infringing substitutes existed, plaintiff may be entitled to lost profits on only a portion of infringing sales equal to plaintiff's share of the relevant market; plaintiff must prove by more-likely-than-not that it would have made that portion of sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not necessary that plaintiff and defendant were the only two suppliers; burden remains on plaintiff to show it would have sold that portion absent defendant's product. In a two-supplier market, plaintiff must show competition and likely sales capture. (Cites Federal Circuit cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor — capacity (manufacturing and marketing ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove it had the manufacturing and marketing ability to supply the additional patented products needed to make the lost sales (or that someone working with plaintiff could have supplied them), and the ability to market and sell those additional products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require proof that plaintiff could have made and sold the additional units during the damages period. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — amount calculation (incremental income approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by computing lost sales for the patented product and subtracting additional costs that would have been incurred to make those lost sales (additional production, sales, packaging, shipping costs). Do not subtract fixed costs that do not change with volume (taxes, insurance, rent, administrative overhead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits cannot be speculative but need not be proved with unerring certainty. (Cites case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — price erosion damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may recover additional damages for price erosion if it shows by more-likely-than-not that but for defendant's infringement it would have charged higher prices (or not lowered prices). Damages equal difference between profits at higher price and profits actually made at the lower price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If awarding price-erosion damages, the higher price may be used in calculating lost sales and lost profits, but must account for any decrease in sales that higher price might have caused. Plaintiff need not have known defendant's product infringed if plaintiff reduced price to meet defendant's prices. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — cost escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may recover additional damages if plaintiff shows by more-likely-than-not that its costs (e.g., increased marketing costs) went up as a result of defendant's infringement and not for some other reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove causal connection between defendant's actions and increased costs. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — collateral sales
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patented product is ordinarily sold with other 'collateral products', plaintiff may recover lost profits for lost sales of collateral products only if plaintiff proves (1) it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement and (2) the collateral products are so closely related that they act or are used together for a common purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages for lost collateral sales are calculated like lost profits for the patented product. (Cites case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — doubts resolved against infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts about damages arising from defendant's failure to keep proper records should be resolved in favor of the plaintiff; confusion/difficulties caused by defendant's records should be held against defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when defendant's recordkeeping prevents exact proof; plaintiff benefits from doubts. (Cites cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If lost profits are not proven for all infringing sales, jury must consider a reasonable royalty — the reasonable amount that someone wanting to use the patented invention would have agreed to pay; damages may not be less than a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable royalty compensates for use of invention; jury should consider evidence of economic value of patent and other relevant factors. (Cites statute and case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — hypothetical negotiation method
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between plaintiff and defendant just before the infringement began. Assume the parties understood the patent was valid and infringed and both were willing to enter into a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'hypothetical negotiation' is a legal fiction used to value the patent at the time infringement began; jury should imagine what a willing licensor and prudent licensee would have agreed upon. (Cites Federal Circuit precedent including Uniloc, Lucent, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 1: established royalties received by licensor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any royalties actually received by the licensor for licensing the patent-in-suit, which may prove or tend to prove an established royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past licenses and royalties are direct evidence of the marketplace value of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 2: defendant's rates for comparable patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the rates paid by the defendant to license other patents comparable to the asserted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable licenses involving defendant can indicate what defendant would pay and what market rates look like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 3: nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a license would be exclusive or non-exclusive, restricted or unrestricted territorially, or restricted with respect to whom the manufactured product may be sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope and exclusivity materially affect royalty valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 4: licensor's policy to maintain exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the licensor's established policy and marketing program to preserve exclusivity (e.g., not licensing others or licensing under special conditions to preserve exclusivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensor's licensing strategy and market behavior bear on reasonable royalty determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 5: commercial relationship between parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the commercial relationship between the licensor and licensee, such as whether they are competitors in the same territory and line of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive relationships may affect bargaining power and royalty terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 6: effect on sales of other products (collateral sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the effect of selling the patented product in promoting sales of other products of the licensee; the existing value of the invention as a generator of sales of non-patented items and extent of such collateral sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral benefits can justify higher royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 7: patent duration and license term
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the duration of the patent and the term of the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer remaining patent term typically increases royalty value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 8: established profitability and commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the established profitability of the product made under the patent, its commercial success, and current popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is probative of value attributable to the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 9: utility and advantages over prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the utility and advantages of the patented invention over prior modes or devices used for similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of improvement and practical advantages inform valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 10: nature and commercial embodiment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature of the patented invention, the character of its commercial embodiment as produced by the licensor, and benefits to those who have used it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial embodiment and realized benefits affect economic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 11: extent of defendant's use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which the defendant has made use of the invention and any evidence showing the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of use by defendant may correlate with appropriate royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 12: customary portion of profit or selling price
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of the profit or selling price that is customary in the relevant business to allow for use of the invention or analogous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry norms for royalty splits and profit allocation are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 13: portion of profit attributable to patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of the profit that arises from the patented invention itself as opposed to profit from unpatented features (manufacturing process, business risks, infringer's improvements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate profits attributable solely to patented features from other sources of profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 14: opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the opinion testimony of qualified experts regarding valuation and economic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert economic testimony may be weighed to estimate a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 15: the hypothetical agreement amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the amount that a licensor and licensee would have agreed upon at the time infringement began if both sides were reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach agreement — i.e., the amount a prudent licensee would pay and a willing patentee would accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor encapsulates the hypothetical negotiation concept: what a prudent licensee would pay while still making a reasonable profit and what a willing licensor would accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty factor 16: any other economic factor a prudent business would consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any other economic factor that a normally prudent business person would, under similar circumstances, take into consideration in negotiating the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catch-all for other relevant economic evidence not specifically enumerated; jury may consider such factors in addition to the listed ones.
